$comment: The curriculum spine. Drives scripts/gen.mjs (images, via gpt-image-bridge → gpt-image-2) and scripts/yt.mjs (video curation). Ordered as a learning path, not a reference index. 'authored' entries are diagrams a human must draw — deliberately NOT generatable; see content/visual-grammar.md §5. Image prompts are dense on purpose: gpt-image-2 takes no reference images here, so the text carries all style consistency.

concepts.title: The Four Forces
concepts.oneLiner: Everything an aircraft does is four arrows arguing with each other.

concepts.$comment:
── PART II — AIR COMBAT ─────────────────────────────────────────────
Chapters 13-20. See PART-II-SPEC.md. Two rules bind harder here than in Part I:
(1) NO HERO MAY DEPICT A GEOMETRY. Not two aircraft in relative position, not a
merge, not an intercept, not a turn circle. A generated tactical relationship
will be wrong and a reader will read it as data. Heroes are weather, distance
and light — nothing that could be mistaken for a claim. (2) Every doctrinal term
in the lessons carries a provenance status; the vocabulary here is part
standardised, part squadron habit, part simulator folklore.
concepts.title: The Three Numbers
concepts.oneLiner: Every fight is one question asked three ways: how far, how far off, and closing how fast.
concepts.misconception: That a dogfight is a sequence of moves you choose, like a fighting game. It is not. Every named manoeuvre is one answer to a problem stated in range, angles and closure — and the same manoeuvre is right or wrong depending entirely on those three numbers.
concepts.secondMisconception: That there is one thing called 'angle'. There are three, and they answer different questions. Aspect is WHERE YOU SIT, measured from the target's tail without any reference to where you are pointing. Angle-off is HOW YOUR HEADINGS COMPARE — the angle between the two aircraft's longitudinal axes. Antenna train angle is HOW FAR YOUR OWN NOSE MUST MOVE to point at them. Collapsing the first two is the specific error, because 'angle off' sounds positional and is not.
concepts.$terminologyWarning: The services do not agree here and the lesson must say so rather than pick one. USAF (MCH 11-F16 Vol 5) defines angle-off as heading crossing angle; the Navy intercept syllabus (CNATRA P-825) uses 'angle off' for the nose-to-line-of-sight angle that the USAF calls antenna train angle. Navy work is done in Target Aspect, measured from the bandit's NOSE; USAF in Aspect Angle, from the TAIL — and TA + AA = 180. 'Angle to target' is NOT a published term and must not be used as though it were; the published term is antenna train angle.
concepts.concrete: Following a car through traffic. You are tracking three things without naming them: how far ahead it is, how far off your nose it sits, and whether the gap is closing.

concepts.title: Three Ways to Point
concepts.oneLiner: Lead, pure, lag. Where you put your nose decides what you gain and what you spend.
concepts.misconception: That you point at the target. Close in and at similar speed, pure pursuit generates closure you cannot spend and drives you straight to an overshoot. It is the right answer in exactly two places — the moment you employ a weapon, and a long-range conversion into someone's rear quarter — and the wrong one in between.
concepts.secondMisconception: That lead pursuit and a lead turn are the same thing. One is where your nose is pointing right now; the other is a decision to start turning before you have passed.
concepts.concrete: Intercepting someone walking across a room. Walk at them and you arrive behind them. Walk at where they are going to be and you meet them.

concepts.title: Rate and Radius
concepts.oneLiner: You can turn fast or you can turn tight. One speed gives you the most of both, and it is nowhere near your top speed.
concepts.misconception: That faster is better in a turn. Past corner speed you are limited by the airframe rather than by the wing: the extra speed buys you radius you do not want and rate you cannot have.
concepts.concrete: Swing a weight round on a string. Short string, and you are limited by your own arm — you cannot make the circle any tighter than your reach. Let it out and speed up, and eventually the string is at its breaking strain: from there, the only way to go faster is to let the circle get bigger. Below that speed your arm is the limit; above it, the string is. The tightest, quickest circle is at the speed where the two limits meet.
concepts.$anchorNote: The bicycle was rejected after fact-checking. A bicycle is grip-limited — its maximum lateral acceleration is roughly the same at every speed, so turn rate rises and radius shrinks all the way down as you slow, and there is NO interior optimum. It would have taught the exact opposite intuition in the one chapter that turns on there being a best speed. The string works because the available turning force genuinely grows with speed, which is the mechanism corner velocity depends on.

concepts.title: One Circle or Two
concepts.oneLiner: At the merge you choose which fight you are in, and you choose it before you arrive.
concepts.misconception: That one-circle is a radius fight and two-circle is a rate fight. Those are tendencies, not rules. Which one favours you depends on your aircraft against theirs, not on the geometry by itself.
concepts.$serviceSplit: Accuracy rule 3 applies here and the chapter must say so out loud. The Navy syllabus (CNATRA P-825) states it flatly as a rule: a one-circle fight IS a radius fight, a two-circle fight IS a rate fight. The USAF handbook (MCH 11-F16 Vol 5) treats it as matchup-driven — it shows fighting one-circle WITH a rate advantage, lists one-circle benefits that are about missile minimum range and unpredictability rather than radius, and says there may not be a single best way to fight any given bandit. Present both; do not pick one and let it read as universal.
concepts.concrete: Two people meeting head-on in a narrow corridor. Both step the same way, or both step opposite ways — and those are completely different problems, decided in the same instant.

concepts.title: Energy Is a Rate, Not a Number
concepts.oneLiner: Speed and height are one thing in two currencies, and every turn presents a bill. Whether you pay it is the fight.
concepts.misconception: That energy fighting means going fast. Specific excess power is a rate: you can be fast and losing, or slow and gaining. The faster aircraft is frequently the poorer one.
concepts.concrete: A bank balance against an income. The balance is what you have; the income is whether it is growing. Rich and haemorrhaging can be the worse position — but not always, because a big balance spent right now still buys something. What matters is that the balance alone never tells you who is winning.

concepts.title: When It Goes Wrong
concepts.oneLiner: Overshoot and the fight can turn over. There are two kinds, and only one of them means you have traded places.
concepts.misconception: That an overshoot means you have lost. A flightpath overshoot and a 3/9-line overshoot are different events. The first is usually a geometry problem you can correct — unless it happens close, fast and at high angle, when the defender can reverse on it. The second is you flying out in front, and that is a change in who is offensive.
concepts.concrete: Overtaking on a motorway. Drifting a little wide of your lane is a correction, and you make it without much thought. Sailing past the car you were following is a different event entirely: it is now behind you, watching you, choosing when to move — and you cannot see it without turning your head.

concepts.title: The Same Geometry, Fifty Miles Out
concepts.oneLiner: Beyond visual range is the same three numbers, decided before you can see anyone.
concepts.misconception: That BVR is a different skill from BFM. It is the same range, angles and closure problem with a radar instead of your eyes and a missile instead of a gun — a crank is lag pursuit flown for the missile's benefit as much as your own, because it shrinks the other side's engagement zone at the same time as it keeps your radar on them.
concepts.secondMisconception: That crank and F-pole are the same thing, and that beaming and notching are the same thing. A manoeuvre is not a distance, and an aspect is not the doppler rejection that beam geometry is usually used to achieve.
concepts.concrete: Turning your shoulder to someone across a crowded room. You have not left, you can still see them, and you are closing at a walk instead of a run.

concepts.title: Deciding Before You Arrive
concepts.oneLiner: Commit, sort, shoot, crank, decide, merge. Every rung is a place to be wrong, and you climb most of them blind.
concepts.misconception: That the fight starts at the merge. The published intercept timeline is a ladder of range-gated tasks — commit, label, sort, shoot, crank, decide — and almost all of it is done before anyone has seen anything at all.
concepts.secondMisconception: That Short, Long and Quick Skate are three separate manoeuvres. In the current brevity publication they are modifiers of one call. Skate is launch-and-leave; Banzai is launch-and-decide; and what separates them is decided before the shot rather than improvised after it.
concepts.concrete: A chess clock. The move you play is fast; everything that decided it happened while the clock was running and nothing appeared to be going on.
